author: john-foxe
fields.title: Foxe’s Book of Martyrs (For Teens)
fields.description: An old bishop who said Christ had never once wronged him. A teenage queen who prayed on the scaffold. A translator who wanted a ploughboy to know the Bible. An archbishop who signed his faith away and then took it back. A missionary’s Bible translation hidden in a prison pillow. This teen edition retells some of the most famous stories from Foxe’s Book of Martyrs, told honestly but without gory detail, including the hard truth that Christians have sometimes persecuted each other, and what these stories mean for following Jesus today.
fields.hook: True stories of ordinary people who would not give up Jesus, even when it cost them everything.

qa.question: Who was John Foxe?
qa.answer: An English writer, born around 1516, who fled England when Queen Mary began burning Protestants. In exile he collected letters, trial records and last words of the martyrs, and in 1563 he published them as the Actes and Monuments, known ever since as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs. He died in London in 1587.

qa.question: What is a martyr?
qa.answer: The word comes from the Greek for “witness.” A martyr is someone who is killed because they would not deny their faith. The first Christian martyr was Stephen, in Acts 7.

qa.question: Is this book against Catholics?
qa.answer: Foxe was a Protestant writing at a bitter time, and his book is often harsh about the Catholic Church. This retelling tells the stories honestly but also says plainly that Protestants persecuted people too, and that today Catholic and Protestant Christians are brothers and sisters who should never treat each other that way.

qa.question: Are the stories violent?
qa.answer: Many of the martyrs were killed in cruel ways. This teen edition says what happened but leaves out the graphic detail, and focuses on what the martyrs said and believed.

qa.question: Are Christians still persecuted today?
qa.answer: Yes. In many countries Christians still face prison, violence or death for their faith. These old stories can help us pray for them and remember that following Jesus has always had a cost.

qa.question: Is this the full text?
qa.answer: No. It is a retelling for teenagers of a few of the most famous stories, in plain modern words, keeping the martyrs’ own words where they say it best. The full book is also available. The edition used here was edited by William Byron Forbush, who added some later stories that Foxe himself did not write.

fields.title: A Church That Will Not Be Destroyed
fields.body_html:
“And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” — Matthew 16:18 (KJV)

In 1554, a young English scholar named John Foxe climbed onto a ship and fled the country, only just ahead of the officers sent to arrest him. A new queen, Mary, had come to the throne, and she was determined to stamp out the Protestant faith in England. Soon people were being burned at the stake for what they believed.

Foxe ended up poor and in exile in Europe, working as a proofreader for printers. But he did something remarkable. He started collecting everything he could find about the people who were dying for their faith: letters smuggled out of prisons, records of their trials, the last words they spoke. When Mary died and he could return home, he published it all. His enormous book, nearly two thousand pages long, became known as Foxe’s Book of Martyrs. For a long time it was the most widely read book in England after the Bible.

Foxe begins with a promise of Jesus. When Peter said that Jesus was the Son of God, Jesus said he would build his church, and “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” Foxe pointed out three things in that promise. First, that Christ would have a church. Second, that the church would be fiercely attacked. And third:

“That the same Church, notwithstanding the uttermost of the devil and all his malice, should continue.”

That is the theme of every story in this book. Emperors, kings and courts tried their hardest to wipe out people who followed Jesus. They failed. The church kept going, often growing fastest where it was attacked hardest.

A word about what is coming. These are true stories, and many of them end in death. This edition tells you what happened without dwelling on gory details. It also tells you honestly that Foxe was a Protestant writing at a bitter time, and that sometimes Protestants persecuted people too. We will come back to that.

But the heart of these stories is not cruelty. It is courage, the kind of courage that comes from knowing Jesus so well that you would rather lose your life than deny him. Most of the people in this book were ordinary: shopkeepers, students, mothers, old men, teenagers. Foxe wanted them remembered “that the wonderful works of God in His Church might appear to His glory.”

One thing to do this week: look up and read Acts 6:8–7:60, the story of Stephen, the first Christian martyr. Notice what he saw, what he said, and how he prayed for the people who were killing him.

study_questions.question: How did John Foxe collect the stories in his book?
study_questions.answer: While in exile, he gathered letters smuggled from prisons, trial records and the last words of those who died for their faith, and published them when he returned to England.

study_questions.question: What three things did Foxe see in Jesus’ promise in Matthew 16:18?
study_questions.answer: That Christ would have a church, that it would be fiercely attacked, and that despite everything it would continue.

study_questions.question: Why did Foxe write his book?
study_questions.answer: He said he wrote it “that the wonderful works of God in His Church might appear to His glory.”

fields.title: Eighty-Six Years
fields.body_html:
“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” — Philippians 1:21 (KJV)

The first Christians lived under the Roman Empire, and for nearly three hundred years they faced waves of persecution. Following Jesus could cost you your home, your freedom or your life. One of the most famous people who died in those years was an old man named Polycarp.

Polycarp was the bishop, or chief pastor, of the church in Smyrna, a city in what is now Turkey. He was very old, and it is said he had known people who knew the apostle John. When officials came looking for him, he went into hiding, but he was found.

What he did next surprised everyone. Instead of fighting or running, he gave the soldiers who arrested him a meal. Then he asked for one thing: an hour to pray. They let him, and Foxe says “he prayed with such fervency, that his guards repented that they had been instrumental in taking him.” The men sent to arrest him felt ashamed.

He was taken before the Roman governor, who wanted him to save his own life by cursing Christ. The governor said: “Swear, and I will release thee;—reproach Christ.” Polycarp’s answer has been remembered for nearly two thousand years:

“Eighty and six years have I served him, and he never once wronged me; how then shall I blaspheme my King, Who hath saved me?”

Think about that sentence. He wasn’t making a speech about doctrine. He was talking about a relationship. For eighty-six years, through everything life had brought, Jesus had never let him down. How could he turn his back on him now?

Polycarp was condemned and put to death. But his words outlived the empire that killed him.

You probably won’t be asked to choose between denying Jesus and losing your life. But you will face smaller versions of Polycarp’s choice: a moment when saying you follow Jesus will cost you something, a laugh, a friendship, a bit of reputation. The best preparation for those moments is the same as Polycarp’s: to know Jesus so well, over time, that you can say from experience, “He has never once wronged me.”

Paul wrote: for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. Polycarp lived that sentence for eighty-six years, and then he died it.

One thing to do this week: write down three ways Jesus has been faithful to you so far in your life. Keep the list somewhere you will see it. Next time following him feels costly, read it.

study_questions.question: What did Polycarp do when the soldiers came to arrest him?
study_questions.answer: He gave them a meal and asked for an hour to pray, and he prayed so earnestly that his guards were sorry they had arrested him.

study_questions.question: What did Polycarp say when the governor told him to curse Christ?
study_questions.answer: “Eighty and six years have I served him, and he never once wronged me; how then shall I blaspheme my King, Who hath saved me?”

study_questions.question: What made Polycarp’s answer so powerful?
study_questions.answer: It was based on a long relationship with Jesus: after eighty-six years of experience, he knew Jesus had never let him down.

fields.title: Young and Brave
fields.body_html:
“Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.” — 1 Timothy 4:12 (KJV)

It is easy to imagine that martyrs were all old, serious saints like Polycarp. Many weren’t. Some were young adults. Some were teenagers.

Around the year 200, in Carthage, in North Africa, a young married woman named Perpetua, about twenty-two years old, was arrested for being a Christian. With her were others, including Felicitas, a young woman who was expecting a baby, and Revocatus, who was a slave. Think about that group: a woman from a respectable family, a slave and a pregnant young mother, side by side, treated as equals because they belonged to Jesus. In the Roman world that alone was remarkable.

They were taken to the amphitheatre, the great arena where crowds watched animals and gladiators, and put to death there. Foxe records it briefly. What stands out is that none of them gave up their faith to save themselves.

In another wave of persecution, in Lyons in France, Christians were again brought into the arena. Among them was a young woman named Blandina. Foxe describes her as “a Christian lady, of a weak constitution,” meaning she was physically frail. Yet she became famous for her courage. Foxe says that when she was put on display before the wild animals, “by her earnest prayers, she encouraged others.” She wasn’t only thinking about herself. She was strengthening the people around her.

When she was brought out the last time, she was with Ponticus, “a youth of fifteen.” Fifteen. Probably about your age. Foxe says that “the constancy of their faith so enraged the multitude” that the crowd showed them no mercy. Both died faithful.

Why does this matter for you? Because it is easy to think that real, costly faith is for later, when you are older, more mature, more sure. These stories say otherwise. Young people have always been capable of great faithfulness. Paul told the young pastor Timothy not to let anyone look down on him because he was young, but to be an example.

Blandina also shows something important. She was physically weak, but her faith made her strong for others. You don’t have to be the confident, popular or strong one to encourage people. One prayer, one word of courage at the right moment, can steady a friend who is wavering.

One thing to do this week: think of a friend who is having a hard time following Jesus at the moment. This week, do what Blandina did: encourage them. Send a message, pray with them, or tell them what God has been teaching you.

study_questions.question: Who were Perpetua and her companions?
study_questions.answer: A group of Christians in Carthage around 202, including Perpetua, a young married woman of about twenty-two, Felicitas, who was expecting a baby, and Revocatus, a slave. They died together rather than give up their faith.

study_questions.question: What did Blandina do in the arena, though she was physically weak?
study_questions.answer: By her earnest prayers she encouraged the other Christians who were suffering with her.

study_questions.question: How old was Ponticus, and why does this matter?
study_questions.answer: He was fifteen. His story shows that young people have always been capable of great faithfulness.

fields.title: The Morning Star
fields.body_html:
“The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.” — Psalm 119:130 (KJV)

Imagine a world where you couldn’t read the Bible in your own language. Church services were in Latin, which most people didn’t understand. A few scholars and priests could read the Scriptures. Everyone else had to take their word for what it said.

That was England in the 1300s. And one man decided it had to change. His name was John Wycliffe.

Wycliffe was born around 1324 and studied at Oxford, where he became one of the most respected scholars in Europe. He became more and more convinced that the church of his day had drifted far from the Bible, and he said so loudly. He criticised the wealth and laziness of some religious orders, and argued that the Bible, not the church’s leaders, should be the final authority for Christians.

He was seriously ill at one point, and some of the friars he had criticised came to his bedside, expecting him to take back what he had said before he died. Instead, Foxe says, he raised himself in bed and replied: “I shall not die, but live to declare the evil deeds of the friars.”

He recovered, and then he “set about a most important work, the translation of the Bible into English.” It was copied out by hand, because printing hadn’t been invented in Europe yet. People who couldn’t afford a whole Bible copied out single Gospels or letters. Foxe notes that the more the authorities tried to suppress it, the more people wanted it.

Wycliffe died of natural causes, but his followers, called Lollards, were persecuted for years, and some were burned with scraps of Scripture tied around their necks. Later Wycliffe was given a nickname: “the Morning Star of the Reformation.” A morning star shines before the sun comes up. He was a light in the dark, pointing to the day that was coming.

It is easy to take the Bible for granted. You can probably find dozens of translations on your phone in seconds. People suffered and died so that ordinary people could read God’s word in their own language. Psalm 119 says that the unfolding of God’s words gives light, and understanding to the simple. That gift cost a great deal.

One thing to do this week: read a chapter of the Bible every day this week, and before you start, thank God that you can read it in your own language. Choose a Gospel if you are not sure where to begin.

study_questions.question: Why couldn’t most people in England read the Bible in the 1300s?
study_questions.answer: Because it was in Latin, which most people didn’t understand, so only scholars and priests could read it.

study_questions.question: What important work did Wycliffe begin after recovering from illness?
study_questions.answer: The translation of the Bible into English, so that ordinary people could read it.

study_questions.question: Why was Wycliffe called “the Morning Star of the Reformation”?
study_questions.answer: Because, like a morning star that shines before sunrise, he was a light in a dark time pointing to the reform that was coming.

fields.title: A Goose and a Swan
fields.body_html:
“Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.” — Matthew 10:28 (KJV)

Wycliffe’s writings travelled across Europe, and in Prague, in what is now the Czech Republic, they inspired a brilliant young pastor and university leader named Jan Hus (Foxe spells it “Huss”).

Hus was born around 1380 in a village in Bohemia. He studied at the university of Prague and became pastor of the Bethlehem Chapel there, where he preached to huge crowds in the language ordinary people spoke, not Latin. Like Wycliffe, he spoke out against corruption in the church, and he insisted that the Bible was the final authority.

In 1414 the church leaders called a great council in the city of Constance and summoned Hus to answer for his teaching. The emperor gave him a “safe-conduct,” an official promise that he could travel there and back safely. Crowds lined the roads to cheer him as he passed. Hus was amazed: “I thought (said he) I had been an outcast. I now see my worst friends are in Bohemia.”

But when he arrived, the promise was broken. He was arrested, imprisoned, put on trial and condemned. He was told to take back what he had taught. He refused, because he would not deny what he believed the Bible said.

When they chained him for execution, he said with a smile: “My Lord Jesus Christ was bound with a harder chain than this for my sake, and why then should I be ashamed of this rusty one?” Offered one last chance to recant, he answered: “What I taught with my lips I now seal with my blood.”

Then he said something that people would remember a century later. “Hus” means “goose” in his language. He told his executioner:

“You are now going to burn a goose, (Huss signifying goose in the Bohemian language:) but in a century you will have a swan which you can neither roast nor boil.”

About a hundred years later, a German monk named Martin Luther started the Reformation. The book’s editors point out that Luther came “about a hundred years after, and who had a swan for his arms.” Whether or not Hus meant it as a prophecy, the point is clear: you can kill a messenger, but you can’t kill the truth he carried.

Foxe records that Hus sang a hymn as he died, so loudly that he could be heard over the crowd. Jesus said not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Hus believed him.

One thing to do this week: is there something you know is true about Jesus that you find hard to say out loud around certain people? This week, find one natural opportunity to say it, kindly and honestly.

study_questions.question: What was a “safe-conduct,” and what happened to the one given to Hus?
study_questions.answer: An official promise from the emperor that he could travel to the council and back safely. It was broken: Hus was arrested, imprisoned and condemned.

study_questions.question: What did Hus say about the chain used to bind him?
study_questions.answer: That Jesus had been bound with a harder chain for his sake, so why should he be ashamed of this rusty one?

study_questions.question: What did Hus mean by the goose and the swan?
study_questions.answer: “Hus” means goose; he said they could burn a goose, but in a century there would be a swan they could not destroy. People later saw this fulfilled in Martin Luther.

fields.title: Here I Stand
fields.body_html:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29 (KJV)

About a hundred years after Hus, a German monk and university teacher named Martin Luther started asking questions that would shake Europe. He came to believe from the Bible that we are made right with God by faith in Jesus, as a free gift, not by our own works or by paying the church. When he spoke out against the selling of forgiveness, the church leaders and the emperor demanded he take it back.

In 1521 he was ordered to appear before the emperor, Charles V, and the great princes of Germany at a city called Worms. His friends begged him not to go. They remembered what had happened to Hus. Luther’s answer was blunt: he would go to Worms “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; yea, although I knew there were as many devils to resist me as there are tiles to cover the houses in Worms.”

When he stood before the emperor, they pointed to a pile of his books and asked him plainly: would he defend them, or take back what he had written? This was the moment. Luther answered:

“If I be not convinced by testimonies of the Scriptures… my conscience is so bound and captivated in these Scriptures and the Word of God, that I will not, nor may not revoke any manner of thing; considering it is not godly or lawful to do anything against conscience. Hereupon I stand and rest: I have not what else to say. God have mercy upon me!”

You may have heard the more famous version: “Here I stand. I can do no other.” The point is the same. Luther was not being stubborn for the sake of it. He said that if they could show him from the Bible that he was wrong, he would change his mind. But he would not go against what God’s word and his conscience told him, not even to save his life. He added simply: “I am tied by the Scriptures.”

Luther was declared an outlaw. Anyone could have killed him without punishment. But friends kidnapped him on the way home and hid him safely in a castle, where he used the time to translate the New Testament into German so ordinary people could read it.

Peter said, “We ought to obey God rather than men.” Second, conscience must be tied to Scripture, not just to your feelings. Luther’s courage came from being “tied by the Scriptures.” Stand firm on what God says, and be humble enough to be corrected by it.

study_questions.question: What did Luther say to friends who warned him not to go to Worms?
study_questions.answer: That he would go in the name of Jesus Christ even if there were as many devils as there were roof tiles in Worms.

study_questions.question: What did Luther say when asked to take back his writings?
study_questions.answer: That unless he was convinced by Scripture, his conscience was bound by God’s word and he would not take anything back, because it is not right to act against conscience: “Hereupon I stand and rest.”

study_questions.answer: That we should not give way on what we are sure God’s word says just because powerful people disagree, and that our conscience must be tied to Scripture, not just to our feelings.

He came to believe from the Bible that we are made right with God by faith in Jesus, as a free gift, not by our own works or by paying the church. When he spoke out against the selling of forgiveness, the church leaders and the emperor demanded he take it back. In 1521 he was ordered to appear before the emperor, Charles V, and the great princes of Germany at a city called Worms. His friends begged him not to go. They remembered what had happened to Hus. Luther’s answer was blunt: he would go to Worms “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; yea, although I knew there were as many devils to resist me as there are tiles to cover the houses in Worms.” When he stood before the emperor, they pointed to a pile of his books and asked him plainly: would he defend them, or take back what he had written? This was the moment. Luther answered: “If I be not convinced by testimonies of the Scriptures… my conscience is so bound and captivated in these Scriptures and the Word of God, that I will not, nor may not revoke any manner of thing; considering it is not godly or lawful to do anything against conscience. Luther’s courage came from being “tied by the Scriptures.” Stand firm on what God says, and be humble enough to be corrected by it. One thing to do this week: think of an area where you feel pressure to go along with something you believe is wrong. Look up what the Bible actually says about it this week. fields.title: The Ploughboy’s Bible
fields.body_html:
“Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.” — Psalm 119:105 (KJV)

William Tyndale was a brilliant English scholar who knew several languages. In the 1520s it was still illegal in England to translate the Bible into English without the church’s permission. Tyndale believed that was a disaster, and he got into an argument with a learned churchman about it.

At one point the churchman said something shocking: “We were better to be without God’s laws than the pope’s.” Tyndale was furious. Foxe says he replied that if God spared his life, “ere many years he would cause a boy that driveth the plough to know more of the Scripture than he did.”

That was his life’s goal: a Bible that an ordinary farm boy could read and understand. He couldn’t do it safely in England, so he left, and worked in hiding in Germany and the Low Countries. He translated the New Testament from the original Greek into clear, beautiful English, and printed copies were smuggled into England, where the authorities burned every copy they could find.

He was eventually betrayed by Henry Philips, an Englishman who made friends with him in Antwerp, and arrested and imprisoned in a castle at Vilvorde for a year and a half. Even there, people noticed his life. Foxe says the people who guarded him reported that “if he were not a good Christian man, they knew not whom they might take to be one,” and it is said he led his jailer and the jailer’s daughter to faith.

In 1536 he was condemned and put to death. His last words were a prayer:

“Lord! open the king of England’s eyes.”

Not a curse on his enemies. A prayer for the king who had opposed him. And within a few years, the king of England did allow an English Bible to be placed in every church, and much of it was Tyndale’s translation. Many of the phrases you know from the Bible in English, like “Let there be light” and “the powers that be,” come from him.

Tyndale also said this about his work: “I never altered one syllable of God’s Word against my conscience, nor would do this day, if all that is in earth, whether it be honor, pleasure, or riches, might be given me.” He handled God’s word with deep respect, because he knew what it was worth.

The Bible on your shelf or phone was paid for in part by men like Tyndale. The best way to honour that is to read it.

One thing to do this week: pick a book of the Bible you have never read all the way through, perhaps Mark or James, and read the whole thing this week, a little each day. You are the ploughboy Tyndale had in mind.

study_questions.question: What did Tyndale say he would do if God spared his life?
study_questions.answer: He would cause a boy who drives the plough to know more of the Scripture than the learned churchman did.

study_questions.question: What were Tyndale’s last words?
study_questions.answer: “Lord! open the king of England’s eyes.”, a prayer for the king who had opposed him.

study_questions.question: What did his guards say about Tyndale while he was in prison?
study_questions.answer: That if he were not a good Christian man, they did not know whom they could call one.

fields.title: Nine Days a Queen
fields.body_html:
“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.” — Psalm 51:1 (KJV)

Lady Jane Grey was a teenager when she was caught up in a power struggle she didn’t choose. When the young King Edward VI died in 1553, powerful men around her pushed her onto the throne to keep his Catholic half-sister, Mary, from becoming queen. Jane was queen for only nine days before Mary’s supporters won. Jane was imprisoned in the Tower of London, and a few months later she was condemned to death. She was only about sixteen.

Jane was known as one of the most brilliant young women in England, fluent in several languages, and a sincere, thoughtful Protestant Christian. She was offered her life if she would give up her faith. She would not.

On the scaffold she spoke to the crowd. She was honest that accepting the crown had been wrong, though she had not sought it. And then she said this:

“I pray you all, good Christian people, to bear me witness, that I die a good Christian woman, and that I do look to be saved by no other mean, but only by the mercy of God in the blood of His only Son Jesus Christ.”

She also said something remarkably honest about her own failings. She confessed that “when I did know the Word of God, I neglected the same, loved myself and the world.” A sixteen-year-old facing death did not pretend to be perfect. She trusted not in her own goodness, but in God’s mercy.

Then she knelt and prayed Psalm 51, the great prayer of repentance: Have mercy upon me, O God. She gave away her gloves and handkerchief and her prayer book. And when the executioner knelt and asked her forgiveness, as was the custom, Foxe says she forgave him “most willingly.”

There are two things to notice here. First, Jane’s hope was clear and simple: not her family, her learning, her goodness or her title, but “only by the mercy of God in the blood of His only Son Jesus Christ.” That is the hope of every Christian, whatever age they are.

Second, she forgave the man who was about to kill her. That is the way of Jesus, who prayed for those who crucified him. Forgiving people who hurt you is one of the hardest and most Christlike things you can do.

Most of us will never face anything like Jane did. But all of us can learn her honesty about our failings, her clear hope in Christ, and her readiness to forgive.

One thing to do this week: think of someone who has hurt you. This week, ask God to help you forgive them, even if it takes time. If it would be safe and wise, think about how you might show them kindness.

study_questions.question: How did Lady Jane Grey become queen, and for how long?
study_questions.answer: Powerful men pushed her onto the throne when King Edward VI died in 1553, to keep Mary from becoming queen. She was queen for only nine days.

study_questions.question: What did Jane say on the scaffold about how she hoped to be saved?
study_questions.answer: That she looked to be saved “by no other mean, but only by the mercy of God in the blood of His only Son Jesus Christ.”

study_questions.question: How did Jane respond when the executioner asked her forgiveness?
study_questions.answer: She forgave him “most willingly.”

fields.title: Light Such a Candle
fields.body_html:
“Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.” — Matthew 5:14 (KJV)

Under Queen Mary, hundreds of people were burned for their faith in England between 1555 and 1558. They included bishops and scholars, but also weavers, farmers, housewives and young people. Two of the most famous were Nicholas Ridley, who had been Bishop of London, and Hugh Latimer, an old preacher famous for plain, powerful sermons.

Both men had helped lead the Reformation in England. Both were arrested when Mary came to the throne, and both refused to give up what they believed. On 16 October 1555, in Oxford, they were led out together to die.

Ridley was nervous. Latimer was old and frail. But as the fire was lit, the old man turned to his friend and said words that have become some of the most famous in English history:

“Be of good cheer, Ridley; and play the man. We shall this day, by God’s grace, light up such a candle in England, as I trust, will never be put out.”

“Play the man” meant: be brave, don’t lose heart. And Latimer’s prediction came true. Their deaths, and the deaths of so many others, did not stamp out the faith in England. They made people ask why ordinary men and women would rather die than give it up. The candle they lit was never put out.

Notice two things about Latimer’s words. First, he encouraged his friend. Even at the worst moment of his own life, he was thinking about Ridley. That is what Christian friends do: we hold each other up when things get hard.

Second, he said “by God’s grace.” Latimer didn’t claim to be brave in himself. He trusted that God would give them the strength they needed when they needed it.

Ridley, too, thought of others at the end. Foxe records that just before he died, he asked one of the officials to plead with the queen for some poor tenants whose rights he was worried about. Facing death, he was still trying to help people who couldn’t help themselves.

Jesus said his followers are the light of the world, like a city on a hill that can’t be hidden. Ridley and Latimer were light in a dark time. Your light might look smaller: a kind word, honesty when it is easier to lie, courage to be known as a Christian at school. But every candle matters. And some of them are never put out.

One thing to do this week: think of a Christian friend who needs encouragement right now. Be their Latimer this week: tell them, in your own words, “Be of good cheer. God will give you what you need.”

study_questions.question: What did Latimer say to Ridley as they were about to die?
study_questions.answer: “Be of good cheer, Ridley; and play the man. We shall this day, by God’s grace, light up such a candle in England, as I trust, will never be put out.”

study_questions.question: How did Latimer’s prediction come true?
study_questions.answer: Their deaths and those of many others did not stamp out the faith in England; instead, the faith they died for continued and spread.

study_questions.question: What did Ridley do just before he died?
study_questions.answer: He asked an official to plead with the queen on behalf of some poor tenants he was worried about.

fields.title: This Unworthy Right Hand
fields.body_html:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9 (KJV)

Not every story in Foxe’s book is about someone who stood firm from start to finish. One of the most powerful is about a man who failed badly, and then found his courage again.

Thomas Cranmer had been Archbishop of Canterbury, the most senior church leader in England. He had written much of the Church of England’s prayer book, and he was one of the chief leaders of the Reformation in England. When Mary became queen, he was arrested and imprisoned in Oxford. While he was there, Ridley and Latimer were burned.

Cranmer was older and frightened. His enemies knew it. They kept him in prison for a long time, and then offered him his life and his old position back if he would sign a statement denying what he had taught. Foxe describes how they did it step by step: the first paper was vague, and once he signed that, they brought another, and another, until finally he had signed a full rejection of everything he had stood for.

It was a terrible fall. And it didn’t even save him. They had already decided he would die.

On the day of his execution, he was brought into a church in Oxford to read out his denial in public. Everyone expected him to confirm it. Instead, he wept and prayed, and then he told the stunned crowd that the thing that troubled his conscience most was “the setting abroad of a writing contrary to the truth,” all those papers he had signed “for fear of death, and to save my life.” He took it all back. And then he said:

“And forasmuch as my hand hath offended, writing contrary to my heart, therefore my hand shall first be punished; for when I come to the fire it shall first be burned.”

And that is what he did. When the fire was lit, Foxe says, he held out his right hand into the flames first, “frequently exclaiming, ‘This unworthy right hand.’” Then, with the words of Stephen, the first martyr, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” he died.

This story is for anyone who has failed. Maybe you gave in to pressure. Maybe you denied knowing Jesus, or went along with something you knew was wrong. Cranmer’s story says: it is not too late. He failed badly, and at the end, he turned back.

Remember Peter, who denied Jesus three times and was forgiven and restored. God forgives those who come back to him. If you have failed, don’t hide it and don’t give up. Confess it, turn back, and stand again.

One thing to do this week: if there is a time you gave in to pressure and went against what you believe, bring it to God this week. Confess it honestly, receive his forgiveness, and ask him for courage next time. If it is right to put something right with a person, do it.

study_questions.question: How did Cranmer’s enemies get him to deny his faith?
study_questions.answer: They kept him in prison and offered him his life and position, getting him to sign one statement after another, each going further, until he had signed a full denial.

study_questions.question: What did Cranmer do on the day of his execution, instead of confirming his denial?
study_questions.answer: He publicly took back all the papers he had signed out of fear and declared that the hand that had signed them would be punished first.

study_questions.question: What does Cranmer’s story teach about failure?
study_questions.answer: That even after a serious failure it is not too late to turn back to God, confess, receive forgiveness, and stand again.

fields.title: When Protestants Did It Too
fields.body_html:
“Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.” — Matthew 7:12 (KJV)

So far, most of the persecutors in this book have been Roman emperors or Catholic authorities. If that were the whole story, you might conclude that one group of Christians were always the villains and the other always the heroes. That would not be true, and Foxe’s book itself shows it.

In the 1650s a new group of Christians arose in England called the Friends, nicknamed “Quakers.” They had some unusual beliefs and practices, and many people disliked them. The editors of Foxe’s book admit that writers had often treated them “in a very contemptuous manner,” and add: “that they did not deserve such treatment, is equally certain.”

Some Quakers went to the American colonies. In Boston, Massachusetts, which had been founded by Puritans, strict Protestants who had themselves fled persecution in England, the authorities passed harsh laws against them. A law from 1656 called them “a cursed sect of heretics.” Ship captains who brought Quakers in could be fined. People who sheltered them were fined for every hour. Quakers were whipped, imprisoned and banished.

And then it went further. The book records that some were banished on pain of death if they returned, and that “four were actually executed by the hands of the hangman.” In October 1659 three were sentenced to death together: William Robinson, a merchant from London; Marmaduke Stevenson, a countryman from Yorkshire; and a woman named Mary Dyer. Robinson and Stevenson were hanged in Boston, and Mary Dyer was hanged there the following year. They were put to death by Protestant Christians, for their faith.

This is uncomfortable. People who had suffered persecution became persecutors when they gained power. And it happened on every side of Christian history: Catholics persecuted Protestants, Protestants persecuted Catholics, and both persecuted other groups like the Quakers and the Anabaptists.

Even Foxe himself, a Protestant who had fled from the fires, saw the danger. In 1575, when two Anabaptists were sentenced to be burned under the Protestant Queen Elizabeth, he begged her to spare them. He wrote: “I have no favour for heretics, but I am a man and would spare the life of a man.”

What should we learn? First, humility. No group of Christians has a perfect record. Second, the Golden Rule: do to others what you would want them to do to you. Christians who have been treated unjustly should be the first to defend others from injustice, even people they disagree with.

And third, today Catholic and Protestant Christians are brothers and sisters in Christ. Whatever our real differences, the right response to these stories is never suspicion or hatred of other Christians. It is to love one another, pray for one another, and never use power to force anyone’s faith.

One thing to do this week: think of a Christian from a different church tradition than yours, Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant or another. This week, pray for them and their church by name, and if you can, ask them about their faith and listen.

study_questions.question: Who persecuted the Quakers in Boston, and what happened?
study_questions.answer: Protestant Puritan authorities passed harsh laws against them; Quakers were fined, whipped, imprisoned and banished, and four, including Mary Dyer, were executed.

study_questions.question: What did John Foxe himself say when two Anabaptists were sentenced to death in 1575?
study_questions.answer: “I have no favour for heretics, but I am a man and would spare the life of a man.”

study_questions.question: What three lessons does this chapter draw?
study_questions.answer: Humility, because no group of Christians has a perfect record; the Golden Rule, defending others from injustice; and love between Christians of different traditions, never using power to force anyone’s faith.

A law from 1656 called them “a cursed sect of heretics.” Ship captains who brought Quakers in could be fined. People who sheltered them were fined for every hour. Quakers were whipped, imprisoned and banished. And then it went further. The book records that some were banished on pain of death if they returned, and that “four were actually executed by the hands of the hangman.” In October 1659 three were sentenced to death together: William Robinson, a merchant from London; Marmaduke Stevenson, a countryman from Yorkshire; and a woman named Mary Dyer. Robinson and Stevenson were hanged in Boston, and Mary Dyer was hanged there the following year. They were put to death by Protestant Christians, for their faith. This is uncomfortable. People who had suffered persecution became persecutors when they gained power. And it happened on every side of Christian history: Catholics persecuted Protestants, Protestants persecuted Catholics, and both persecuted other groups like the Quakers and the Anabaptists. Even Foxe himself, a Protestant who had fled from the fires, saw the danger. In 1575, when two Anabaptists were sentenced to be burned under the Protestant Queen Elizabeth, he begged her to spare them. He wrote: “I have no favour for heretics, but I am a man and would spare the life of a man.” What should we learn? First, humility. No group of Christians has a perfect record. Second, the Golden Rule: do to others what you would want them to do to you. Christians who have been treated unjustly should be the first to defend others from injustice, even people they disagree with. And third, today Catholic and Protestant Christians are brothers and sisters in Christ. Whatever our real differences, the right response to these stories is never suspicion or hatred of other Christians. It is to love one another, pray for one another, and never use power to force anyone’s faith. One thing to do this week: think of a Christian from a different church tradition than yours, Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant or another. This week, pray for them and their church by name, and if you can, ask them about their faith and listen.

fields.title: A Pillow in Prison
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.” — Hebrews 13:3 (KJV)

The edition of Foxe’s book in our library includes some later stories, added long after Foxe died. One of them is about the first American missionaries sent overseas, and it begins in a haystack.

In 1806 a group of students at Williams College in Massachusetts were caught in a thunderstorm and sheltered by a haystack. They used the time to pray for the world, and decided that if they could, they would go as missionaries themselves. This “haystack prayer meeting,” as it came to be called, led to the founding of the first American missionary society. One of the young men who soon joined them was Adoniram Judson.

Judson and his wife Ann sailed for Asia and, in 1813, settled in Rangoon, in Burma (now Myanmar). They learned the language and began translating the Bible into Burmese. It was slow, hard work, and for years very few people became Christians.

In 1824 war broke out between Britain and the Burmese emperor. Because Judson was a foreigner, he was arrested in Ava, the capital, as a suspected spy, and thrown into a terrible prison with other foreigners. For many months he was kept in chains, in heat and filth, often close to death.

Ann Judson became his lifeline. Foxe’s edition includes her own letter describing those days. She walked to the prison again and again, bringing food, pleading with officials, bribing guards, and caring for him, all while expecting, and then caring for, their baby daughter Maria. She became seriously ill herself, and at one point nearly died.

And through it all, one precious thing was protected: Judson’s translation of the New Testament into Burmese, years of work. The book says it “was put into a bag and made into a hard pillow for Dr. Judson’s prison.” He had to act as if it didn’t matter, so the guards wouldn’t take it. With the help of a faithful Burmese Christian, the manuscript survived.

Judson was eventually released when the war ended, after about two years of suffering. The Burmese Bible he finished is still used today, and the church in Myanmar now numbers in the millions.

The Bible says to remember those in prison as if you were in prison with them. Christians are still imprisoned for their faith in many countries today. Like Ann Judson, we can’t always set them free. But we can remember them, pray for them, and support those who help them.

One thing to do this week: find out about one country where Christians are persecuted today. Pray for the Christians there by name every day this week, and ask your church or youth group how you might support them.

fields.title: A Great Cloud of Witnesses
fields.body_html:
“Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.” — Hebrews 12:1 (KJV)

We have met an old bishop, a slave and a young mother, a frail woman and a boy of fifteen, a scholar, a preacher, a translator, a teenage queen, two friends at the stake, an archbishop who failed and stood again, persecuted Quakers, and a missionary couple in a Burmese prison. What do we do with all these stories?

The book of Hebrews, after listing many faithful people from the Old Testament, says that we are surrounded by “so great a cloud of witnesses.” The word for witness in Greek is martys, which is where our word martyr comes from. These people are like a crowd in a stadium, cheering on the runners who come after them. And that is us.

Here are some things these witnesses say to us.

Courage comes from relationship. Polycarp could stand firm because he had walked with Jesus for eighty-six years. The best preparation for hard moments is a real, daily friendship with Christ now.

God’s word is worth everything. Wycliffe, Hus, Luther and Tyndale risked or gave their lives so that ordinary people could read and trust the Bible. Don’t let it gather dust.

Failure is not the end. Cranmer fell, and stood again. If you have given in, you can come back.

Honesty about our own side. Christians have persecuted Christians, and Protestants did it too. Real courage includes humility and love for believers who are different from us.

And, above all, Jesus is worth it. Every person in these stories decided that Jesus was worth more than safety, comfort, reputation or even life. They weren’t superhuman. Many were frightened. They simply trusted that Jesus was who he said he was, and that what he promised was real.

Hebrews goes on: let us lay aside every weight and run with patience the race set before us, “looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross.” The martyrs kept their eyes on Jesus, who suffered first.

You probably won’t face fire or prison. But you will face your own race, with its own costs. When you do, remember the crowd in the stands. They are cheering for you. And the One they died for is running with you.

One thing to do this week: choose the one story from this book that moved you most. Write a short prayer asking God to give you the same faith, and pray it every day this week.

study_questions.question: What does “cloud of witnesses” mean in Hebrews 12:1?
study_questions.answer: The faithful people who have gone before us, pictured like a crowd in a stadium cheering on the runners who come after them.

study_questions.question: Where does the word “martyr” come from?
study_questions.answer: From the Greek word for “witness.”

study_questions.question: What is the most important thing all the martyrs in this book believed?
study_questions.answer: That Jesus was worth more than safety, comfort, reputation or even life, because he is who he said he is and what he promised is real.
